title: Annotatio II §.II: Becanus’s personal/perichoretic union; In/Cum/Sub + Verborgen → Impanation suspicion
pass_a_gloss: Becanus (Manual of Controversies bk. 2 ch. 2 q. 2 p. 330) expounds at length that Luther inculcated the latter — namely a personal, and so intimate and perichoretic, Union of Christ’s body with the bread — in two senses. And truly Luther by his own formulas of speech generated no light suspicion of either mode asserted by him, when on the one hand he explained Christ’s words This is my body both in prose by these three particles In, With, and Under this bread is my body, and in a bound Song composed by himself — Jesus Christ our Savior &c. — by this rhythm, hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — and gave amplest occasion for loading that Explanation with the titles Impanation and Companation.
pass_b_english: Becanus (Manual Controv. II.2.2 p. 330) charges Luther with a personal, intimate, perichoretic union of body with bread.

Luther’s own speech feeds the suspicion: In, With, and Under this bread is my body, plus his hymn line hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — ample handle for Impanation and Companation labels.
source_text: Posteriorem, Unionem scil. corporis Christi cum pane personalem, eoque intimam & perichoristicam, Lutherum inculcasse in duobus sensibus, prolixius exponit Becanus, Manual. Controv. lib. 2. cap. 2. quest. 2. p. 330. Et sanè vero Lutherus utriusque modi à se asserti, formulis suis loquendi, haud levem suspicionem genuerit, quando ex una parte, verba Christi, hoc est corpus meum, tùm in prosa oratione, per tres has particulas, In, Cum, & Sub hoc pane est corpus meum, tum in ligata Cantione à se composita: JEsus Christus unser Heyland &c. / per hunc rythmum, verborgen im Brod so klein / gab Er uns seinen Leib zu essen / explanavit, hancque suam Explanationem Impanationis & Companationis titulis gravandi ansam dedit amplissimam.
